cards.headline: Six people killed and about 30 injured in Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in Gaza

pages.text: An Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, killed six people and injured approximately 30 others, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. The strike hit a building containing surgical wards and intensive care units overnight, with the hospital's director stating that two missiles struck the structure, though one did not explode. Among those killed were surgeon Dr. Rizq Abu Shaira and a 13-year-old boy, according to Gaza's education ministry. British surgeon Goher Rahbour, who was volunteering at the hospital, reported that the strike occurred just after midnight, shook the entire building, and left the recovery area on the fourth floor reduced to rubble. A paramedic from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency stated in a social media video that a missile penetrated the five-storey structure and hit a room in the surgical department.

The Israeli military confirmed the attack, stating it targeted a senior commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who used the hospital as a headquarters to plan attacks against its forces. Dr. Ayman Abu Obeid, head of surgery at the complex, rejected this account, stating there were no armed men or fighters inside the hospital building. Hamas accused Israel of spreading false narratives in an attempt to cover up a war crime. Israel has accused Hamas of exploiting civilian infrastructure by storing weapons and running command and control rooms in hospitals, a claim Hamas denies. While hospitals have protected status under international law, they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war. Because Israel does not allow international news organizations, including the BBC, into Gaza, it is difficult to independently verify developments in the territory. The Nasser Medical Complex is the largest hospital in southern Gaza and serves almost one million people.

cards.headline: Russia attacks Kyiv with missiles and 123 drones following trilateral peace talks

pages.text: Russia launched an onslaught against Kyiv using ballistic missiles and 123 attack drones hours after a round of trilateral peace talks mediated by the United States concluded in Abu Dhabi. The attacks occurred following negotiations between Russia and Ukraine that reportedly ended with little progress due to heated debates over territory and Europe's participation in future discussions. While both sides agreed to prepare another major prisoner swap, the talks faced significant friction regarding land ownership and national sovereignty.

Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko reported that Ukraine shot down 94 attack drones and no missiles during the strike. The attack resulted in one death and five injuries in Kyiv. Emergency services also reported fires in the Rivne and Zhytomyr regions. Additionally, Moscow reported shooting down approximately 70 Ukrainian drones over eight regions overnight. Russia’s defense ministry claimed responsibility for the attack, stating it targeted electricity substations and drone production sites. However, Moscow also struck residential districts in the Ukrainian cities of Kremenchuk and Chernihiv, which killed multiple civilians, including children.

During a press conference in Dublin on November 11, 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that territory remained a central topic of discussion. Zelenskyy noted that mediators from the U.S. focused on various ways to resolve the territorial dispute, particularly regarding the Donbas region. He said the Russians suggested that stopping the war might require Ukraine to leave its own territory, adding that it is impossible to negotiate in a way that compromises the country's independence. A senior official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss classified details, noted that one idea discussed was the potential administrative transfer of parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions to a different oblast if the war stopped along the current front line, though the official clarified this does not mean Ukraine would recognize the occupied territories as Russian.

cards.headline: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigns following court rulings on educational credentials

pages.text: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has tendered his resignation to parliament, triggering a process to find a replacement for the office. The resignation follows a Supreme Court ruling that a high school document used during his 2024 election campaign was invalid, amid controversy over whether his qualifications met the legal requirements to run for office. Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated. The court stated that no evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification. This ruling followed a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October that reached the same conclusion. Gibran, 39, had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his credentials after studying in Singapore and Australia.

President Prabowo Subianto told reporters he accepted the resignation with a “heavy heart,” stating that Gibran had demonstrated “a chivalrous attitude, a strong sense of responsibility, and the qualities of a statesman.” Prabowo added that the resignation was “for the benefit of the nation, the state, and the people of Indonesia.” Regarding the educational dispute, Prabowo said that while Gibran believes he completed his education through a proper and structured process, the president noted that “educational systems abroad differ from those in Indonesia.” Gibran had reportedly offered to resign on November 10, 2026, during a meeting with the president to avoid prolonged political controversy, though a cabinet minister said Prabowo urged Gibran at that time to defend himself.

The resignation occurs amid a faltering political alliance between President Prabowo and former President Joko Widodo, Gibran's father. On November 11, 2026, a petition submitted to the leaders of the House of Representatives by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties began a parliamentary process that could lead to Gibran’s impeachment. Under Indonesian law, House leaders must establish a special committee to examine whether Gibran violated the constitution by serving despite allegedly failing to meet election requirements. If lawmakers find sufficient basis for the accusation, the House must ask the Constitutional Court to rule on whether a constitutional violation occurred. Former President Widodo told reporters from his hometown in Solo that political positions are temporary and stated, “We will continue to support President Prabowo’s government, especially programmes that serve the interests of the broader public.”

cards.headline: South Africa's ANC vows soul-searching after worst-ever local election performance

pages.text: Leaders of South Africa's ruling African National Congress (ANC) met at a special National Executive Committee meeting to discuss the party's future following its worst performance at the ballot box in local government elections. The party's vote share dropped 15 percentage points to 31 percent. The ANC's secretary-general described the result as a “catastrophic outcome” and stated the party would enter a period of “soul-searching” to determine how to win back the trust of the South African people. This follows a national election two years ago where the ANC lost its parliamentary majority after receiving 40 percent of the vote; the party previously viewed that result as a disaster and an opportunity for self-reflection, though supporters have continued to desert the organization. The ANC once commanded 70 percent of the vote without challengers.

Despite the election losses, ANC national spokesperson Mahlengi Bhengu-Motsiri stated that President Cyril Ramaphosa will not resign. To maintain influence in local government, the ANC must engage with other political parties to form coalition governments in municipalities where no single party secured an outright majority. Bhengu-Motsiri said the National Executive Committee will receive reports on initial engagements with other parties and consider the adoption of a mandating guide. This guide is intended to set the mandate for the ANC’s appointed negotiations team.

cards.headline: Houthis deny targeting Mecca as fighting intensifies in Yemen

pages.text: The Iran-allied Houthi group has rejected claims from Saudi Arabia that it targeted the holy city of Mecca, even as fighting intensifies between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government. On November 11, 2026, a Houthi spokesperson denied what he called Saudi “lies” regarding a drone launch toward Mecca. The spokesperson stated instead that a drone was launched at a pumping station in Yanbu on the Red Sea and that three cruise missiles targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. Earlier, Saudi-led coalition forces reported intercepting three cruise missiles aimed at Riyadh, along with drones directed toward Mecca and southern regions of Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence Authority reported that debris from the interception of two ballistic missiles fell in the village of Sabuhah in Mecca province. The Civil Defence Authority described the targeting of civilian objects as a flagrant violation of international humanitarian law. According to the World Health Organisation, more than 320,000 people have been displaced in Yemen due to fighting since August 1.

Inside Yemen, combat has escalated between Houthi fighters and the Saudi-backed army representing the internationally recognised government. Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili, the spokesperson for Yemen’s army, reported that at least 138 Houthi fighters were killed or wounded in hundreds of targeted attacks. In a post on X, al-Nuzaili stated that the Saudi-backed army conducted 773 field artillery attacks, 44 drone strikes, and 37 rocket attacks across the al-Jawf, Marib, al-Bayda, and Taiz governorates. He also noted that Saudi-led coalition forces carried out 23 air strikes against the Houthis, which damaged 86 heavy weapons and military vehicles. Despite these operations, Saudi-backed forces have not stopped Houthi attacks on the al-Buraiqa district in Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based. Minister of Information Salem al-Awalqi stated on social media that the repeated shelling of the densely populated al-Buraiqa district reflects a pattern of the Houthi militia targeting civilians.

cards.headline: Spanish parliament passes housing reforms following nationwide strike

pages.text: Spain’s interim lower house of parliament has ratified housing measures intended to limit evictions and real estate speculation to make housing more affordable. The approval comes one day after a nationwide general strike over the country’s housing crisis. The duration of these reforms will depend on the outcome of a snap election scheduled for later in November. The leading opposition party, the conservative Popular Party, has stated it will repeal the measures of the left-wing government if it takes power, an outcome that current polls indicate could happen.

The legislative push follows national uproar after the death in October of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen. Televised images of her eviction from her home in September shocked many Spaniards and prompted large demonstrations across the country. Protest camps emerged in several cities, with the largest located in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square. In response to the parliament's previous failure to pass decrees providing greater tenant protection against evictions and the automatic renewal of tenant contracts, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a general election, which had been scheduled for 2027.

On November 11, 2026, hundreds of thousands of Spaniards participated in a 24-hour walkout over soaring rents and the high cost of living. Trade unions called the strike after previous decrees were blocked. In Barcelona, municipal police estimated that more than 55,000 people took part in the demonstration, while organizers placed the figure closer to 400,000. While the mass demonstration was described as otherwise peaceful, violent clashes erupted in the city center when groups of masked protesters began throwing stones, bottles, and fireworks at police near Passeig de Gràcia and Plaça de Catalunya. During the unrest, rubbish bins and street furniture were set alight, shop windows were smashed, and stores were reportedly looted. Catalonia's Mossos d'Esquadra police moved to disperse the groups as disturbances spread toward Las Ramblas. Eighteen people were arrested during the unrest, bringing the day's total to 20 arrests. Catalan President Salvador Illa condemned the violence, stating it did not reflect the spirit of the peaceful protest.

cards.headline: Trump says US does not need a deal to end war with Iran and redirects Vance to domestic issues

pages.text: President Donald Trump has stated that the United States is no longer seeking a deal to end the war with Iran, ordering Vice President JD Vance to focus on domestic politics instead. Trump, who had previously empowered Vance to negotiate, announced the shift via a post on his Truth Social platform, stating, “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” This move effectively normalizes a stalemate with Iran. Following the announcement, oil prices rose and Wall Street futures slipped further.

The conflict began in February when the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran. In response, Iran closed access to the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for energy transit, which caused a steep increase in the cost of fuel globally. While the US has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports and has mostly reopened the Strait of Hormuz to marine traffic, including crude oil shipments, the war has entered a period of relative inactivity. The US has not carried out massive strikes against Iran for several months, and Iran has not launched barrages of ballistic missiles against US bases and allies in the region. During a White House press conference, Trump said the war was “effectively over” and that Israel and Gulf allies were well protected, noting that an escalation was not needed.

Trump is redirecting Vance, who had been speaking to intermediaries in Iran and Qatar about restarting negotiations, to focus his “complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.” This redirection follows reports that Vance was considering face-to-face talks with a top Iranian security official. The shift in focus comes after the Republican Party experienced sweeping losses in midterm elections, with Democrats gaining control of Congress. Some Republicans, including Vance, have blamed the Iran war and its impact on fuel prices for those electoral losses.

cards.headline: Russian President Vladimir Putin meets with U.S. envoys at the Kremlin

pages.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin met with envoys from U.S. President Donald Trump at the Kremlin to discuss the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff traveled directly to the Kremlin following two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates. Washington sought to provide new momentum to peace efforts after these talks failed to yield visible progress toward ending nearly five years of large-scale hostilities, despite concluding with an agreement on a large-scale prisoner exchange.

The meeting in Moscow follows the first direct talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials in nine months. While the negotiations in the United Arab Emirates resulted in the prisoner exchange agreement, they did not produce progress toward ending the war. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned European leaders against discussions between the United States and Russia regarding a new security agreement for the continent. On November 6, 2026, U.S. negotiators met with both Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

cards.headline: Two Iranian men convicted in London of spying on dissident journalists

pages.text: A London court has convicted two Iranian citizens of spying on reporters for Iran International, a Persian-language television station critical of the Iranian government. The Woolwich Crown Court found the men, both in their 40s, guilty of conducting surveillance on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). One of the convicted men was also found guilty of plotting a violent attack against one or more of the journalists, while the second man was convicted only of spying. A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges. Sentencing for the convicted men is scheduled for mid-December. Iran has repeatedly rejected the allegations against the men, who were arrested following investigations into hostile activity in the United Kingdom. During the proceedings, one defendant claimed he acted under duress because his family had been threatened, while the other stated he did not know his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence. British counterterrorism police stated the case reflects intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, noting a recent security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase, a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force. The defendants were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the IRGC, a multi-discipline military force in Iran that is considered closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than the regular armed forces. The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, a designation that allows for penalties of up to 14 years in prison for those supporting or assisting the organization under new rules regarding national security and state threats.

cards.headline: Fugitive former MP Ranjit Chandra Sarkar allegedly held secret meeting in Sylhet

pages.text: A police case in Bangladesh has revealed that Ranjit Chandra Sarkar, a former member of parliament for Sunamganj-1 who has been in hiding since 5 August 2024, secretly held a meeting with party activists at a resort in the Ratargul area of Gowainghat, Sylhet. The meeting, which took place at 8pm on 8 November at Sohel Square Resort, allegedly involved leaders and activists of the banned Awami League, the Chhatra League, and their affiliated and associate organisations. Police allege the gathering was intended to create instability in the country, bring down the government, and plan acts of violence, including setting fire to and vandalising roads and government offices in Gowainghat upazila. Ranjit Chandra Sarkar, the former organising secretary of the Sylhet district unit of the Awami League, was named as the chief guest on a banner seized from the resort and is listed as the fifth accused in the case.

Gowainghat Police Station filed the case under the Anti-Terrorism Act on 11 November 2026. The case, filed by Sub-Inspector Naimul Islam, names 20 people and accuses another 175 unidentified individuals. On 11 November 2026, police arrested 15 people during raids at various locations in Gowainghat. During a raid at the resort at approximately 1:50am, police arrested two people attending the meeting and seized a banner, seven empty liquor bottles, and 40 metal objects resembling airgun pellets. Other named accused in the case include Faruk Ahmed, general secretary of the banned Awami League's East Alirgaon union unit in Gowainghat; Ali Hossain, a member of the banned Jubo League's East Jaflong union unit; and Ekhlasur Rahman, also known as Tara Mia, organising secretary of the banned Awami League's Tahirpur upazila unit. While Sarkar was the former MP for Sunamganj-1, the case states the meeting occurred in Gowainghat, Sylhet. No senior official of the Sylhet district police has commented on Sarkar's current whereabouts, though he is described as a fugitive in the case. Political speculation in Sylhet has suggested Sarkar left the country across the border nearly two years ago.

cards.headline: President Mahama unveils $10 billion New Economy Programme for Ghana

pages.text: President John Dramani Mahama has outlined a $10 billion, four-year New Economy Programme intended to transform the structure of the Ghanaian economy. The programme, which anchors the 2027 budget, aims to build an economy that produces more of what it consumes, processes more of what it grows, and earns more from its exports to the world. Speaking at the Bank of Ghana during the launch of the Ghana Cedi Heritage Series, President Mahama stated that the programme is designed to create local jobs and reduce the need for the country to spend foreign exchange on goods that can be produced competitively within Ghana.

President Mahama linked the success of the New Economy Programme to the stability of the Ghanaian Cedi. He explained that expanding and diversifying exports would increase foreign exchange inflows, while increasing domestic production would reduce dependence on imports. According to the President, these efforts, combined with disciplined public finance and credible monetary policies, are intended to create a stronger currency capable of withstanding global shocks. He noted that the programme is central to providing the Cedi with a firmer economic foundation.

cards.headline: 53 countries and organizations urge incoming Israeli government to open Gaza for winter aid

pages.text: Fifty-three countries and international organizations, led by the United Kingdom, Qatar, and Jordan, have called on Israel’s incoming government to lift restrictions on fuel, medical supplies, and shelter materials entering Gaza. The group warned that displaced Palestinians face threats from hypothermia, respiratory infections, and waterborne diseases as winter approaches. The statement was directed at the new Israeli government, which is expected to emerge in the coming weeks following elections in Israel. The signatories urged Israeli authorities to allow Egyptian and Jordanian humanitarian corridors to operate fully and predictably, and to approve a wider range of critical aid items, including those currently classified by Israel as “dual-use”—items with legitimate civilian applications that could also be used in military operations.

cards.headline: Ghana government to invest $1 billion in Pwalugu Multipurpose Dam

pages.text: The government of Ghana plans to invest US$1 billion to complete the Pwalugu Multipurpose Dam, a project intended to increase agricultural production, expand agro-processing, and strengthen the energy supply. Finance Minister Dr. Ato Forson announced the investment while presenting the 2027 Budget Statement in Parliament. The project is part of the government's New Economy Programme, which aims to transform commercial agriculture, strengthen local industries, and create employment opportunities. The dam is expected to be implemented in phases, with the first phase scheduled to be ready by early 2029 and full completion planned for December 2030.

The dam is designed to support several industrial and agricultural functions across the White Volta corridor. According to Dr. Forson, the project will provide water for approximately 25,000 hectares of land for vegetable production and its reservoir is intended to accommodate 100,000 fish cages for aquaculture. Additionally, the dam is expected to generate 77 megawatts of hydropower. This electricity is intended to power irrigation systems, processing factories, pack houses, and cold storage facilities to help businesses add value to agricultural produce near production centers. The project is also expected to provide flood protection, improve water security, and promote year-round agricultural production.

cards.headline: Finland to restrict entry for Russian athletes due to war in Ukraine

pages.text: Finland will restrict Russian athletes from entering the country because of the war in Ukraine, a move that could affect multiple winter sports. The Finnish foreign ministry stated the measure will apply to Russians competing for national teams as well as those competing under neutral status. This decision follows backlash in Finland regarding the reinstatement of Russia for the ice hockey world championships. Elina Valtonen, the Minister for Foreign Affairs, said, “As long as Russia’s war of aggression continues, Russian athletes have no business in Finland.” Valtonen added that their entry would threaten Finland’s international relations and noted that the same applies to other non-essential short-term work under visas that does not serve Finland’s national interests.

Skating and cross-country skiing are expected to be the first sports affected by the restrictions. Finland hosts a figure skating grand prix and a cross-country ski World Cup, both of which allow Russians to compete as “neutral athletes.” One major event potentially impacted is the figure skating world championships in March, where Russian skaters are expected to be among the top medal contenders. The International Skating Union (ISU) stated that it believes athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments while many conflicts are ongoing, and the organization is seeking clarifications from skating officials in Finland.

cards.headline: Russia and Iran cooperate to evade US efforts to stop weapons shipments via the Caspian Sea

pages.text: A joint assessment by the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and the Critical Threats Project (CTP) states that Iran and Russia are cooperating to counter United States efforts to block weapons shipments to Iran through the Caspian Sea and land routes. The study notes that Iran has used Caspian Sea trade routes with Russia to import Russian arms both before and during the 2026 US-Israel-Iran War. This activity prompted Ukraine to strike a shipment in July 2026. According to the think tank's analysis, the Caspian Sea remains outside the reach of Western monitoring bodies, which allows sanctioned Russian cargo ships to move consignments from the ports of Astrakhan and Olya to the Iranian ports of Anzali, Nowshahr, and Amirabad.

An examination of recent maritime traffic data shows that sanctioned Russian cargo ships transfer cargoes to the Iranian ports of Anzali, Nowshahr, and Amirabad after loading in Astrakhan and Olya. As these ships approach the shores of the two countries, they switch off their Automatic Identification Systems (AIS)—a tracking technology used to identify and locate vessels—to conceal the nature of their cargoes. Last summer, Ukraine's Security Service announced that long-range drones targeted two cargo ships in the Caspian Sea which, according to Kyiv, were involved in transferring military equipment between Iran and Russia. Tehran and Moscow have sought to deepen security and military ties while expanding economic and transit relations through the North-South corridor.

A flagship project for both nations involves completing the Rasht-Astara railway, a transit route intended to connect Russia to ports in the Persian Gulf. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, stated following a recent meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow that the council approved the executive agreement for the railway's construction. Rezaei added that the meeting included discussions on building gas pipelines from Russia to Iran to address fuel shortages and enable exports to neighboring countries. These developments occur as the security situation in the Strait of Hormuz remains volatile. The public relations office of the Revolutionary Guard Navy reported that two supertankers, carrying more than four million barrels of oil in total, were involved in an incident involving a massive explosion while passing through the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz.

cards.headline: Hundreds of thousands expected to protest in Prague over Czechia public media reform

pages.text: Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague's Letna Park this weekend to protest the Czech government's efforts to pass a bill reforming public media funding. The proposed legislation has already triggered strikes and demonstrations across Czechia, but this gathering is expected to be the largest to date. A massive protest is also scheduled to take place in Prague on November 15. The unrest follows a surprise overnight session in which the populist coalition of Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, resulting in a vote of approval at 04:36 a.m. on October 24.

The government's proposal would scrap the current license fee model used to fund Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo), replacing it with direct funding from the state budget. The three parties in the coalition—Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and the radical conservative Motorists—argue the license fee is an unfair tax. They claim the new arrangement would make the broadcasters more efficient, noting that funding for CT and CRo would be cut by around 15% in the first year. The coalition also points to similar changes made in other European Union states as a precedent.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations, and international watchdogs have accused the government of attempting to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has reportedly irked ANO and the SPD. While analysts note that other EU models include guarantees for editorial independence and long-term financial stability, they point out that the Czech government proposal offers neither.

cards.headline: United States and experts call for crackdown on illegal mining as 60 percent of Ghana's freshwater sources face degradation

pages.text: The United States and scientific experts have issued an urgent call for a crackdown on galamsey, or illegal small-scale gold mining, in Ghana. The demand follows reports that mercury-driven pollution has degraded an estimated 60 percent of the country's freshwater sources, according to figures from the Water Resources Commission of Ghana cited by Sarah Cobb of the U.S. Bureau of Oceans and International Environmental and Scientific Affairs (OES). During a symposium in Accra on November 10, 2026, experts warned that the pollution threatens public health, food security, and economic opportunity. Specifically, mercury exposure can harm developing brains, heart tissue, and cause reproductive effects for pregnant mothers and their babies. The symposium, titled “Addressing Mercury Pollution: Collaborative Solutions for Sustainable Mining in Ghana,” was organized by the U.S. Embassy on behalf of the Regional Environment, Science, Technology, and Health Hub for West and Central Africa to unite various sectors in reducing mercury use.

Environmental assessments highlight the severity of the contamination. A 2024 baseline assessment by the U.S. Geological Survey in the Western Region found that total mercury in unfiltered water from the Ankobra and Pra rivers was more than 55 times higher than the U.S. average, while river sediments were two to 25 times higher. In the Birim River, turbidity—a measure of water cloudiness—linked to mining pollution reportedly reached 63 million Nephelometric Turbidity Units (NTU), far exceeding the maximum treatable level of 200 NTU. This level of contamination left a community water treatment plant unable to function. Sarah Cobb noted that mercury does not remain at mine sites but moves through rivers into sediment, where it builds up in fish and eventually reaches farm products and drinking water.

To address the crisis, Cobb urged the government to enforce the law and fund restoration, the industry to adopt clean technologies, and scientists to use data to inform decisions. She acknowledged existing Ghanaian efforts, including a five-step anti-galamsey plan and a drone-equipped command centre operated by the Minerals Commission, as foundations for achieving results. Cobb also called for sustained support from development partners to help mitigate the damage to Ghana's rivers before it becomes irreversible.

cards.headline: Scent-detecting mule from British Columbia joins private search for missing woman in Arizona

pages.text: Sonny, a scent-detecting mule from British Columbia, and his handler, Marion Weiskopff, have joined a private search to find Chelsea Grimm, who vanished in 2023. Grimm disappeared while on a cross-country road trip, and her vehicle was found abandoned on a forest service road in the Kaibab National Forest, located just south of the Grand Canyon in Arizona. Private investigator Steve Fischer, who is working the search for Grimm, learned about Sonny through contacts in the search-and-rescue community. Weiskopff is a volunteer with Princeton Ground Search and Rescue (PGSAR), part of British Columbia's only dedicated mounted search-and-rescue team. While the team is mounted, this is the first time Sonny has been utilized for his scent detection skills.

Sonny developed his scenting abilities at training clinics in Oregon and Arizona several years ago and has won equine scenting competitions in both states. In 2024, Sonny and Weiskopff received an award for winning a scenting field trial in Oregon. Weiskopff described Sonny's process, stating that when he picks up a smell, he stops moving, sniffs the air, and turns toward the source of the scent. During a trial, Weiskopff noted that Sonny found a scent in a 10-acre plot in under a minute and a half, whereas other horses often take 10 minutes or longer.

cards.headline: Flooded shelters and high prices leave Gaza families struggling to stay warm

pages.text: Families in Gaza City, Gaza Strip, are struggling to keep children and vulnerable relatives warm as winter approaches, facing flooded makeshift shelters and high prices for clothing and blankets. In a makeshift camp west of the city, 27-year-old Amira Saad lives with 18 family members, including nine children, under a tarp that provides little protection from the elements. The family was previously displaced from the Shujayea neighbourhood in Gaza City during the war between Israel and Palestine. Recent heavy rain flooded their shelter while they were sleeping, soaking mattresses, pillows, and blankets.

Amira Saad reported that her four-month-old baby, Mohammed, mostly has only thin summer clothes. While she borrowed a warm garment from a neighbour, she remains worried about the cold at night. Other children in the household mostly have old, torn summer clothes. Additionally, 60-year-old Basima Saad, Amira's mother-in-law, expressed concern for her 23-year-old daughter, who has a disability and requires both warm clothing and medication. Basima Saad stated that the daughter's hands become as cold as ice, leading her to keep the woman beside her in bed to provide warmth.

cards.headline: Holland Bloorview in Toronto launches food support program for caregivers

pages.text: Holland Bloorview, a children’s rehabilitation hospital in Toronto, has started a comprehensive hospital-based food support program to provide meals for parents and caregivers during long inpatient stays. According to a hospital news release, the initiative is the first of its kind in Canada. Previously, hospital treatment coverage only included meals for patients, leaving caregivers to manage their own food costs and planning while supporting children in care. The new program provides $30 a day to caregivers of inpatient clients for hot meals on weekdays and grocery credits on the weekends. Sue Osbourne, a social worker at Holland Bloorview, said the program aims to reduce the financial and mental burden of arranging meals during stressful periods, allowing caregivers to access the hospital cafeteria without prior planning. Osbourne noted the program addresses significant local needs, stating that one in five families at the hospital report experiencing household food insecurity and 6 per cent of families receiving care live below the poverty line. cards.headline: Stellantis sale of Brampton auto plant to Roshel ends 40 years of automaking

pages.text: Stellantis has sold its Brampton, Ontario, assembly plant to the defence contractor Roshel Inc., ending 40 years of automotive manufacturing at the facility northwest of Toronto. The sale follows a period of idled operations that began in late 2023 when the automaker halted production to retool the plant for the Jeep Compass. That retooling process was paused in early 2025 after President Donald Trump imposed 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars, leading Stellantis to shift Jeep Compass production to Belvidere, Illinois. The sale leaves approximately 3,000 employees who were sent home during the 2023 idling in a state of uncertainty regarding their employment.

Unifor chairperson Ardis Snow, a 38-year Stellantis employee, described the sale as devastating for workers who have been waiting for years to return to their jobs. Snow stated that laid-off workers face mental-health challenges and financial hardship, noting that some have sold their houses and moved. Unifor national president Lana Payne called the sale an “unacceptable outcome” and the “worst-case scenario” for the union and its members. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown also criticized the development, with Carney calling the sale a “betrayal” to Canadians.

Roshel Inc. CEO Roman Shimonov stated the company plans to employ thousands of people and will give first priority to the workers who lost their jobs in Brampton. However, laid-off worker Baltej Bajwa expressed concern that Roshel's production capacity will be far fewer than the 400 to 800 vehicles that the 2,200 Stellantis workers produced daily. Bajwa said that while the job opportunities are helpful, the sale leaves the remaining portion of the workforce in a state of disarray. Local businesses have also felt the impact of the plant's closure; Shelly Lewis, owner of Shelly's Kitchen, reported having to lay off a staff member as foot traffic dwindled following the 2023 idling.

cards.headline: Border control pilot launched to stem drug smuggling into five First Nations in northern Ontario

pages.text: The Nishnawbe Aski Police Service (NAPS) has launched a border control pilot program to prevent the smuggling of drugs and alcohol into five First Nation communities in northern Ontario. The initiative comes as the Nishnawbe Aski Nation (NAN)—a political territorial organization representing 49 First Nations across Treaties 9 and 5—remains in a state of emergency due to drug trafficking and related violence. NAPS, which is the largest Indigenous police force in Canada, has recruited special constables from the participating communities to conduct searches of all travellers entering the five First Nations. These searches are conducted based on rules established by each community’s own Band Council Resolutions, which are formal decisions made by a community's governing body. The concept for the program originated in August 2022, when chiefs with NAN directed NAPS to develop a dedicated search program to prevent illegal drugs from entering NAN communities.

Solomon Atlookan, Chief of Eabametoong First Nation, stated that individuals from the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) use various methods to smuggle drugs into the remote Ojibway community in northwestern Ontario. Atlookan noted that drugs are sometimes transported via float planes down the river, while in colder months, trucks bring them in using winter roads. He also said traffickers often conceal drugs on their bodies at the airport to exploit limited security. Additionally, Atlookan said unknown individuals enter the community and make friends with members to facilitate deliveries. Atlookan described the program as an effort to manage very limited resources to prevent drug influx, noting that the trafficking has resulted in the deaths of young people and caused suffering for families and children.

cards.headline: Two men found guilty of assisting Iranian intelligence in attempts to eliminate UK-based journalists

pages.text: Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, have been found guilty of assisting Tehran’s intelligence services in a plan to “eliminate” targets in the United Kingdom. The two men of Iranian origin carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March in an attempt to inflict violence on specific individuals. The targets included Jonathan Turner, a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, and two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini. According to Woolwich crown court, the defendants visited addresses linked to the targets, took photos and videos, and used the AI platform ChatGPT to research them online.

The case involved the use of social media to hire proxies—individuals who work for foreign security forces, often with little knowledge of who they are targeting or why. Sepahvand used ChatGPT to locate the home address of Pourmohsen. Court proceedings heard that Sepahvand hoped to be paid £150,000 to carry out a violent attack to help “finish off” Pourmohsen. In December 2024, Sepahvand used WhatsApp to communicate with his handler, an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander identified as Amin, while spying on Pourmohsen. During these communications, Amin sent messages such as, “These are new pictures of the guy/bloke,” and asked, “And that dot is their office?”

Sepahvand and Manesh entered the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022; Sepahvand arrived in the back of a lorry and Manesh arrived in a small boat. This case follows a similar instance where 19-year-old Norwegian Johannes Natland was jailed for life after agreeing to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organized crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

cards.headline: Ghana risks importing potable water as mercury pollution threatens rivers

pages.text: Ghana faces the risk of having to import safe drinking water within the next two years if mercury pollution from artisanal and small-scale mining is not addressed. Experts warned that communities in several mining areas, specifically Tarkwa and its environs, could be forced to import potable water due to increasing river pollution. During a symposium that ended on November 11, 2026, speakers called for a paradigm shift to reduce mercury use and promote sustainable mining practices. Dr. Sylvester Akpah, Chief Executive Officer of Smart Innovation Ghana Limited, stated during a research presentation that between 42.5 and 62 tonnes of mercury are used annually in Ghana’s artisanal and small-scale mining sector.

The adoption of mercury-free gold processing technology has stalled across major gold-producing areas despite government investment. In June 2022, the government commissioned approximately 100 mercury-free gold processing machines. The Minerals Commission indicated that the government spent US$10 million to procure these machines to promote responsible mining and environmental stewardship. However, many miners struggle to afford the equipment, which was procured at US$113,000 each under a work-and-pay arrangement. A mercury-free gold catcher is a device that uses water to wash away sand and trap heavier gold particles from crushed ore without using mercury. This technology is intended to protect miners' health, prevent toxic vapour emissions and water pollution, and allow gold recovery without exposing the environment to mercury.

The discussion regarding these environmental and public health risks took place at a two-day forum organized by the U.S. Embassy in Accra. The event was held on behalf of the Regional Environment, Science, Technology and Health Hub for West and Central Africa under the Ambassador’s Water Experts Programme (AWEP). The forum brought together government officials, academia, civil society, development partners, and private-sector representatives to discuss immediate measures to reduce mercury use.

cards.headline: Shigellosis outbreak among Montreal's unhoused population raises alarm for shelter workers

pages.text: A severe stomach bug is spreading through Montreal's homeless population, prompting concerns from shelter workers regarding the adequacy of containment efforts. The infection, known as shigellosis, is caused by bacteria and results in fever, stomach cramps, and diarrhea. While the infection can typically be prevented through hygiene practices like handwashing, many unhoused individuals lack consistent access to washrooms and clean water.  Julien Montreuil, head of the group L'Anonyme, which works with people in encampments, stated he believes the situation is currently under control, though he noted that basic hygiene advice from public health officials can be complicated for those living in tents.

Shelter staff have expressed varying perspectives on the response to the outbreak. An employee at the Old Brewery Mission, one of the city's largest shelters, reported the situation to the province's workplace safety board and stated that employees do not feel the matter is being taken seriously enough or that current measures are sufficient. The worker requested anonymity due to concerns for job security.  In eastern Montreal, Michelle Patenaude, executive director of CAP Saint-Barnabé, said her organization, which operates three shelters, has taken precautions to curb the bacteria's spread. Patenaude noted that she was at one point forced to restrict access to some services and emphasized that the organization does not take the situation lightly, noting that infection prevention is a major challenge in the collective environments where they welcome vulnerable people daily.

cards.headline: CITES lifts trade sanctions against Laos, prompting conservation concerns

pages.text: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), a global wildlife trade regulator, has lifted trade sanctions against Laos. This decision allows the Southeast Asian nation to resume trade of species such as long-tailed macaques without special restrictions. The CITES Standing Committee announced the move in Geneva, stating that Laos has made “significant progress” in addressing issues that led to the sanctions in 2023. Those original sanctions were imposed due to the country's failure to regulate tiger and bear bile farms and its inability to rein in criminal networks trading illegal wildlife products with near-impunity. While the sanctions are lifted, the review process for Laos has not ended, and ongoing monitoring of the country's adherence to CITES rules will determine its ability to continue exporting species listed under the convention.

Some conservationists have called the decision “premature,” arguing that Laos must do more to curb an illegal wildlife trade estimated to be worth billions of dollars annually. In 2025, a joint investigation by Mongabay and the NGO GI-TOC identified 35 illegal wildlife shopping sites in Vientiane and Luang Prabang that sold products including pangolin scales, rhino horn, and ivory to Chinese tourists. While the number of these shops had grown by July 2026, sources monitoring the trade in Laos told Mongabay that most had closed shortly thereafter, with only six or seven believed to be operational as of August 2026. Somvang Phimmavong, director-general of Laos’ Department of Forestry, told Mongabay that authorities inspected 25 shops, ordered six to close, and detained 27 foreign nationals. In an email to Mongabay, Phimmavong stated, “We recognize that sustained progress requires continued investigations, prosecutions, demand reduction and effective oversight of wildlife facilities.”

cards.headline: Space dust grains provide evidence of ancient heavy-oxygen water reservoir in the Kuiper belt

pages.text: Researchers have found evidence in space dust that has entered Earth's atmosphere suggesting an ancient reservoir of water enriched with heavy oxygen isotopes exists in the Kuiper belt. The Kuiper belt is a region beyond Neptune containing icy bodies composed mostly of frozen water, methane, and ammonia mixed with rock and dust. These objects have escaped much of the processing experienced by objects closer to the sun, such as the rocky and metallic asteroid belt. While scientists have long predicted a primordial supply of heavy-oxygen water might exist in the outer solar system, they previously lacked evidence because testable samples from that region are rare. A study published in Science Advances describes how 12 grains of dust can provide information about the conditions in the outer solar system.

The findings center on oxygen isotopes, which are different forms of the element. Oxygen has three stable isotopes: light oxygen, which has eight protons and eight neutrons, and two heavier variants that have eight protons and either nine or 10 neutrons. When these heavier isotopes of oxygen combine with hydrogen, they form a type of heavy water. While evidence of this heavy water has been previously found in minerals from one primitive meteorite and in the comet 67P, it was previously unclear if heavy water was common throughout the outer solar system or if those findings were exceptions.

cards.headline: Ocean carbon sink strengthens while land carbon sink stalls, study finds

pages.text: An international study has found that the ocean is absorbing increasing amounts of carbon dioxide, while the amount taken up by land ecosystems has remained unchanged for more than 30 years. This research highlights the growing role of oceans in regulating the global carbon cycle through carbon sinks—natural systems that provide a net uptake of carbon from the atmosphere. Using more than 30 years of atmospheric oxygen and carbon dioxide measurements, researchers were able to distinguish between the amounts of carbon absorbed by land and the ocean. The study was led by the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California San Diego and co-authored by experts from the University of Exeter. Between 1990 and 2019, the ocean absorbed an average of 2.8 billion tonnes of carbon each year, which is equivalent to approximately 35 per cent of fossil fuel emissions during that period. The ocean carbon sink strengthened by approximately 0.63 billion tonnes of carbon per decade.

In contrast to the ocean, the net land carbon sink showed no notable long-term increase. Land ecosystems absorbed an average of around one billion tonnes of carbon each year between 1990 and 2019, equivalent to approximately 13 per cent of fossil fuel emissions. The land sink peaked around 2009 and has generally declined since. These findings challenge existing land models that predict increasing carbon uptake as rising nitrogen and atmospheric carbon dioxide stimulate plant growth. The researchers noted the trend is striking because current estimates suggest emissions from land-use changes and deforestation have been declining. The results also show the ocean sink has strengthened substantially more than is represented in current model simulations, suggesting scientists may lack a complete understanding of how the carbon cycle behaves under future climate change. Professor Andrew Watson, one of the Exeter researchers, stated that while the parts per million precision required for atmospheric oxygen measurements is incredibly difficult to achieve, the work provides a unique understanding of how the Earth system responds to human-caused change.

cards.headline: New research suggests comets may not have delivered the ingredients for life to Earth

pages.text: New research suggests that a longstanding theory—which posits that comets delivered the molecular ingredients necessary to kickstart life when they struck Earth during its youth—is extremely unlikely. In a study published October 28 in the journal Scientific Reports, researchers used computer simulations to model the delivery of organic molecules via comets and found that successful deliveries to Earth would have been rare, if not impossible. While the findings reorient discussions regarding the origin of life on Earth, the researchers suggest that Mars may be a slightly more likely destination for comets to have delivered biologically useful organic molecules.

The research team, led by Richard Anslow, a planetary scientist at the University of Cambridge in England, investigated the potential delivery of hydrogen cyanide (HCN). This molecule, composed of hydrogen, carbon, and nitrogen, was created from leftovers of the solar system’s formation 4.6 billion years ago and has been detected on many comets. HCN can serve as a precursor for essential life building blocks, such as nucleotides, sugars, and lipids, because its carbon-containing organic molecule has an extremely strong chemical bond that can drive subsequent reactions. This bond also makes the molecule very stable and more likely than other organics to survive an impact. Anslow told Science News’ Skyler Ware that if the delivery of hydrogen cyanide looks unlikely, it would be even harder for more complicated molecules to survive, as they are more likely to be broken down during impacts.

cards.headline: Climate adaptation policies in Copenhagen may increase social inequality by disproportionately raising costs for low-income residents

pages.text: A study from the University of Copenhagen suggests that climate adaptation policies may worsen social inequality. While cities invest in infrastructure to manage extreme weather, the financial burden of these projects is not shared equally among residents. In Copenhagen, tenants in not-for-profit housing and apartment buildings shoulder a larger share of the costs compared to owners of single-family houses. This occurs because these neighborhoods are often located near climate adaptation projects. According to Natalie Marie Gulsrud, an associate professor in the Department of Geosciences and Natural Resource Management at the University of Copenhagen and the study's first author, the type of housing a person occupies determines how much of the climate adaptation bill they pay. The study, titled “Housing Tenure, Climate Resilience, and Ecological Segregation,” was published in PNAS.

To combat increasingly severe flooding and cloudburst events, Copenhagen and other cities worldwide invest in infrastructure such as cloudburst tunnels and the separation of stormwater from wastewater. These measures are designed to reduce pressure on sewer systems and are intended to benefit all residents. However, the University of Copenhagen study indicates that these efforts can lead to rising rents. Gulsrud stated that “one-size-fits-all climate adaptation policies worsen urban injustice,” noting that stormwater costs fall disproportionately on residents of not-for-profit housing despite the city's reputation for climate leadership.

cards.headline: Study challenges costs of Alto high-speed rail project in Canada

pages.text: A study by Vision Transport and the Union des producteurs agricoles (UPA), an agricultural group, suggests a rail link between Quebec City and Toronto could be built at a fraction of the estimated cost and environmental impact of the high-speed train project being developed by the Crown corporation Alto. The research was conducted by Pierre DuSablon, a rail industry expert, and Vincent Duguay, a master’s student in research at the École nationale d’administration publique. It examines two scenarios: an express route with stops only in major cities and a route serving the same 22 stations currently used by Via Rail. The authors state that while their proposed modernized route would be slower, it would still be faster than traveling by car. Currently, rail travel from Quebec City to Toronto takes eight hours and 40 minutes, which is slightly longer than driving.

The study's proposed routes offer different travel times compared to Alto's plan, which promises to connect Quebec City to Toronto in four hours and 30 minutes. According to the authors, a modernized route serving intermediate stations like Drummondville or Saint-Hyacinthe would take six hours and 40 minutes, while an express route would take five hours and 50 minutes. Caron questioned whether alternatives with less expense and impact could be considered. cards.headline: Brain scans reveal structural differences in treatment-resistant schizophrenia

pages.text: A study published in the journal Molecular Psychiatry found that individuals with treatment-resistant schizophrenia exhibit specific structural differences in their brains, such as a smaller hippocampus, when compared to patients who respond to standard medications. Schizophrenia is a psychiatric condition involving delusions, hallucinations, and cognitive impairments. Standard antipsychotic drugs typically work by blocking dopamine receptors in the brain to reduce symptoms, but up to 60 percent of patients do not experience adequate relief from these therapies. This lack of response is known as treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Identifying these anatomical variations could eventually allow doctors to recognize which patients are unlikely to benefit from typical antipsychotic drugs, potentially enabling earlier alternative interventions.

Currently, medical professionals diagnose treatment resistance only after a patient fails to improve following multiple trials of different antipsychotic drugs. This trial-and-error process can take months or years, often leading to the deterioration of a patient's mental health during that time. The only medication currently approved for patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is clozapine. However, clozapine requires strict blood monitoring because of the risk of severe immune system complications, and a substantial portion of patients still fail to respond to the drug.

cards.headline: Lemon industry waste produces bioplastic more flexible than commercial standard, study finds

pages.text: Researchers have developed a method to transform lemon processing residues into a biopolymer known as PHBV, which demonstrated greater flexibility than a commercial grade when compared under identical conditions. The study, published in the journal Polymers, investigated using lemon industry byproducts as carbon sources to produce the material using the halophilic archaeon Haloferax mediterranei. This process, referred to as waste valorization, turns industrial waste into higher-value products to address plastic pollution and food waste challenges. The resulting polymer, termed HFX PHBV, showed lower crystallinity and a high hydroxyvalerate content, which enhanced its ductility compared to the commercial PHBV grade Enmat Y1000.

To improve the material's properties, the researchers supplemented the HFX PHBV with nucleating agents—substances that encourage the formation of crystals within a polymer to alter its structure. The study tested orotic acid, boron nitride, and theobromine, finding that orotic acid was the most effective at enhancing crystallization kinetics. The incorporation of these agents improved the mechanical stiffness and crystallization behavior of the PHBV, which researchers say broadens the potential range of applications for the produced biopolymer. The research was authored by Salvador García-Chumillas et al., with CETEC acting as the coordinator for ANIPH alongside partners from the Viss and PHAntastic projects.
